Alleviation of propionic acid inhibition and enhancement of methane 
production in anaerobic digestion by micronano-bubble 
water supplementation
Yujie Fan a, Yuqi Liu b, Ziyang Zhang b, Jinke Sun c, Xiaojing Yang d, Peng Deng a, Haibo Yang a,  
Ziwen Zhao b,*
a College of Forestry, Henan Agricultural University, Zhengzhou, Henan 450002, China
b South China Institute of Environmental Sciences, Ministry of Ecology and Environment, Guangzhou 510345, China
c School of Environmental Science and Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou 510006, China
d School of Civil and Transportation Engineering, Guangdong University of Technology, Guangzhou 510006, China
H I G H L I G H T S
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T
• Micronano-bubble water (MNBW) addi­
tion accelerated propionic acid (HPr) 
degradation.
• MNBW boosted partial and total alka­
linity in anaerobic digestion system.
• Methane production was enhanced by 
13.5%–18.4% with MNBW under HPr 
inhibition.
• MNBW supplementation promote hy­
drolysis and methanogenesis under HPr 
inhibition.
• MNBW improved the tolerance of 
archaea such as Methanosaetaceae to HPr 
inhibition.
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Micronano-bubble water
Propionic acid degradation
Anaerobic digestion
Buffering capacity
Methane production
A B S T R A C T
Micronano-bubble water (MNBW) was used to accelerate propionic acid (HPr) degradation and enhance methane 
production in anaerobic digestion (AD) in this study. Results showed that HPr degradation was accelerated by 
MNBW addition. Moreover, methane production was elevated by 13.5% to 18.4% under HPr inhibition by 
MNBW supplementation. Microbial analysis revealed that MNBW boosted the bacterial populations involved in 
protein and carbohydrate consumption. In addition, supplementation with MNBW improved the tolerance of 
archaea such as Methanosaetaceae to HPr inhibition, thus increasing methane production. MNBW also promoted 
alkalinity recovery, lowered intermediate alkalinity/partial alkalinity and volatile fatty acid/total alkalinity 
ratios, and enhanced buffering capacity. Enzyme activity increased by MNBW, including a 21.0% increase in 
coenzyme F420 and a 7.0% to 13.8% increase in extracellular hydrolase activity. This work highlights that 
MNBW is a promising approach to accelerate HPr degradation, optimize methanogenic pathways, and boost 
methane production.

1. Introduction
Among the various biomass waste treatment technologies, anaerobic 
digestion (AD) is widely recognised for its ability to reduce pollution and 
produce bioenergy, making it applicable across multiple industries (Mo 
et al., 2023). AD offers significant advantages including renewable en­
ergy generation, pathogen inactivation, and odour control (Xu et al., 
2023). However, its effectiveness is often limited by inhibitory factors, 
with volatile fatty acids (VFAs) accumulation being one of the main 
causes of decreased efficiency and lower energy yield. VFAs inhibition is 
a common issue in dry AD process, particularly during the acidogenesis 
stages, when the overproduction of organic acids leads to the accumu­
lation of VFAs (Li et al., 2024b).
As one of the main components of VFAs, propionic acid (HPr) is 
converted to acetate before being consumed by syntrophic propionate 
oxidizing bacteria in the hydrogenotrophic pathway (Eq. (1) to (3)
(Rocamora et al., 2023). The process of HPr oxidation to acetate is prone 
to inhibition problems, because this process is the most thermodynam­
ically unfavoured reaction in the chain (Stams and Plugge, 2009).

CH3COO−+ H+ + 2H2O ↔2CO2 + 4H2

(3) 
HPr is particularly challenging to degrade because of its high energy 
demand, which makes it thermodynamically unfavourable (Cruz Viggi 
et al., 2014). According to a previous study, the accumulation of HPr is 
due to thermodynamic blocking of HPr degradation caused by hydrogen 
partial pressure exceeding 10-4 bar (Rocamora et al., 2023). However, 
some reports suggest that the increased hydrogen partial pressure is not 
the cause of HPr accumulation, but rather a by-product of HPr degra­
dation (Choong et al., 2016; Banks et al., 2012). A lack of trace elements 
like Fe, Ni, Se, W or Co is another cause of HPr accumulation, as they 
enable HPr degradation and the hydrogenotrophic pathway, and are 
necessary for enzymes and direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET) 
required for the relationship between methanogens and syntrophic 
bacteria (Westerholm et al., 2015; Li et al., 2021a). The abundance of 
methanogens consuming acetic acid is influenced by the conversion rate 
of HPr and is ultimately reflected in biogas production (Han et al., 
2020). Accumulation of HPr can lead to acidification of AD system, 
decrease of methanogens activity, and eventually lead to AD system 
collapse (Li et al., 2021b). Therefore, effective HPr degradation is crit­
ical for overcoming HPr inhibition and improving AD efficiency. Various 
strategies, such as the use of nano-magnetite (Li et al., 2021b), nanoscale 
zero-valent iron (Cheng et al., 2020), and FeCl3 (Yang et al., 2024), have 
been explored to enhance HPr breakdown. Although promising, these 
approaches are often expensive, environmentally unsustainable, and 
difficult to scale for industrial applications. It is urgent to develop an 
alternative approach that can fundamentally accelerate HPr degradation 
with a low cost, no secondary pollution, and convenient operation.
One promising technology is micronano-bubble water (MNBW), 
which contains high concentrations of nanobubbles (Liu et al., 2019). 
These micronano-bubbles (MNBs) are gas-filled cavities with diameters 
range from a few nanometers to hundreds of nanometers that exhibit 
unique characteristics (Ghaani et al., 2020). MNBW is widely used in 
many fields, such as medicine and agriculture (Bismuth et al., 2022; 
Marcelino et al., 2023). Previous report has suggested that MNBW is 
beneficial for increasing methane yield (Yang et al., 2019). Fan et al. 
(2020) applied three kinds of MNBW (Air, H2 and CO2) to the AD of SM 
and obtained preliminary experimental results that all three kinds of 
MNBW can significantly increase methane production. Among them, 
Air-MNBW has the lowest cost and the simplest operation. Hou et al. 
(2021) found that the promotion effect of Air-MNBW on methane pro­
duction was higher than that of N2-MNBW. Therefore, Air-MNBW can 
facilitate the AD process while being cost-effective and easy to operate. 
Although the conclusion that MNBW can promote AD has been 
confirmed, these preliminary findings were based on the premise that 
MNBW does not appear to inhibit AD. Given the unique properties of 
MNBW and its positive performance in AD systems, MNBW may have 
the potential to alleviate HPr inhibition. In addition, the use of MNBW to 
accelerate HPr degradation without secondary pollution and the prep­
aration cost of MNBW are low, easy to operate, and has the potential for 
industrial application.
Therefore, this work investigated the use of MNBW to accelerate HPr 
degradation, alleviate VFAs inhibition, and improve methane produc­
tion. This study represents the first exploration of the application of 
MNBW to HPr degradation under inhibitory conditions and provides a 
potential solution to one of the key challenges in AD technology. By 
addressing HPr accumulation, this study aims to contribute significantly 
to the field of renewable energy production through more efficient AD 
processes.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Preparation of substrate, inoculum and MNBW
2.1.1. Substrate and inoculum preparation
In this study, to effectively treat organic waste and prevent envi­
ronmental pollution, we selected swine manure (SM) as the substrate 
because the substrate used in AD should be readily available and cost- 
effective. The SM was obtained from Guigang pig farm, Guangxi Prov­
ince, China. To avoid interference from foreign materials during the 
experiments, impurities such as pig feed were removed from the SM. 
Additionally, to ensure consistency across different experimental 
groups, the SM samples were thoroughly homogenised before use in 
subsequent AD experiments. The digested sludge samples used as inoc­
ulum were sourced from Guangzhou sewage treatment plant, Guang­
dong Province, China. The acclimation procedure was as follows: SM 
collected from the same farm and digested sludge were mixed at a feed- 
to-microorganism ratio of 1:1 (volatile solid [VS] basis) and placed in 1- 
L Schott Duran bottles. The characteristics of the AD substrate and 
inoculum are listed in Table 1. 
2.1.2 Preparation of MNBW
MNBW was prepared using a 6-L MNBW generator (Yuchuang 
Environmental Technology Co., Ltd., Shandong, China), which was 
described in detail in the previous study (Tang et al., 2022). Considering 
the cost and practical application of organic waste treatment, air was 
selected for the preparation of MNBW (Air-MNBW), allowing us to 
source air directly from the natural environment, without the need for 
more expensive gases such as oxygen, nitrogen, or hydrogen. Air was 
introduced into the MNBW generator following a procedure described 
previously (Tang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2019). The flow rates of air and 
deionized water (DW) were set to 0.6 L/h and 3 L/min respectively. The 
pressure was maintained at 0.24 ± 0.01 MPa. The temperature was set 
at 20 ± 1◦C, and the preparation time was 30 min. It can be observed 
that MNBW changes from a milky opaque liquid to a colorless trans­
parent liquid. The prepared MNBW was subjected to a subsequent AD 
process involving SM.
2.2. HPr inhibition batch experimental set-up
In this study, the batch experiments utilized 250 mL Schott Duran 
bottles. The raw substrate and acclimated inoculum were loaded into 
250 mL reactors (R) with a working volume of 200 mL, maintaining a 
feed-to-microorganism ratio (on a VS basis) of 1:1. Each reactor con­
tained 4.65 g SM and 95.35 g inoculum, with a total loading of 100 g. 
Subsequently, 100 mL MNBW was supplemented to MNBW groups and 
the same volume of DW was supplemented to control groups. To

simulate varying degrees of HPr inhibition, equal concentrations (1000 
mg/L) of the HPr standard solution were added to the reactors at 
different volumes according to the results of the preliminary experi­
ment. In addition, in order to better set the HPr inhibition gradient of 
this work, some previous research reports were referred to (Yang et al., 
2024; Li et al., 2021). HPr were added to achieve final concentrations of 
1.25, 2.5, and 5.0 g-HPr/L. According to the final concentration of HPr 
obtained and whether MNBW was added, the batch reactors were 
grouped into eight groups, named Control-0, Control-1.25, Control-2.5, 
Control-5, MNBW-0, MNBW-1.25, MNBW-2.5, and MNBW-5. In addi­
tion, two control bottles containing only the inoculum were tested for 
comparison with the four experimental groups (see supplementary 
material).
To simulate different levels of HPr inhibition and avoid interference 
from acidic or alkaline chemicals, no pH adjustments were made during 
the experiment. This also prevented potential contamination by chem­
ical additives. After ensuring thorough mixing of the materials within 
the reactors, nitrogen (99.9995 %) was applied to purge the 250 mL 
bottles for 3 min. The reactors were sealed using specialised caps. Before 
placing all the reactors in an incubator (35 ± 2 ◦C), all reactors were 
checked to ensure they were properly sealed, and the batch AD experi­
ment was initiated. Three parallel and two replicate experiments were 
conducted. The key AD parameters were measured at regular time 
points.
2.3. Methods of detection and analysis
In this experiment, biogas production was obtained using 50 and 5 
mL syringes and normalized to standard temperature and pressure (1 
atm, 25 ◦C). The biogas composition, including methane and other gas 
components, was analysed according to a previous study with a sample 
volume of 1 mL (Yang et al., 2019). The total solid, VS and total 
ammonia nitrogen (TAN) were determined based on the standard 
methods (APHA 2012). Soluble proteins and carbohydrates were 
measured according to the methods reported in the previous literature 
(Fan et al., 2020). The concentrations of HPr and other components of 
VFAs were analysed according to a previous report (Yang et al., 2019). 
Total alkalinity (TA), intermediate alkalinity (IA), and partial alkalinity 
(PA) were determined according to previously reported methods (Banks 
et al., 2012).
To assess the enzymatic activity during the hydrolysis phase of AD, 
the activities of acid phosphatase, α-glucosidase, alkaline phosphatase, 
and protease were determined on day 4, following the methodologies 
outlined in an earlier report (Goel et al., 1998). Additionally, F420, 
which is closely associated with methanogenic microorganisms, was 
determined according to previously established methods (Gao et al., 
2024). At the end of the experiment, AD sludge samples under different 
HPr inhibition were collected and the microbial community structure 
was subsequently analyzed. During microbial analysis, the E.Z.N.A. Soil 
DNA Kit (OMEGA) was applied to extract genomic DNA. The NanoDrop 
2000 spectrophotometre (NanoDrop Technologies) was used to deter­
mine the purity and concentration (Tang et al., 2024). Samples were 
collected from the reactors for high-throughput sequencing. The 
different sets of primers were used to amplify 16S rRNA for the analysis 
of archaeal communities (524F10extF (5′-TGYCAGCCGCCGCGGTAA- 
3′)/Arch958RmodR (5′YCCGGCGTTGAVTCCAATT-3′)) and bacterial 
communities 
(338F(’5-ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG-3′)/806R 
(5′- 
GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′)). In addition, the raw sequencing data 
has been uploaded to public database. The SubmissionID is 
SUB15017517 and the BioProject ID is PRJNA1212302.

2.5. Statistical analysis
In this study, experimental data on the MNBW promotion of HPr 
degradation and mitigation of acid inhibition were analysed using 
Microsoft Office Excel 2021. The mean ± standard deviation (SD) was 
applied to facilitate subsequent discussion. One-way analysis of variance 
followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test was performed to assess statistical 
differences. Graphing and further data analyses were conducted using 
Origin 9.0.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Variations in HPr and VFAs concentrations
HPr is the main component of VFAs, and its trend during AD is 
closely related to VFAs concentration. Overall, except MNBW-5 and 
Control-5, the VFAs concentration of the other reactors increased first 
and then decreased (Fig. 1a and 1b). For MNBW-5 and Control-5, the 
VFAs concentration remained above 5000 mg/L, indicating severe VFAs 
inhibition. The VFAs concentration of MNBW-2.5 was higher than 
Contol-2.5 on day 4 (p < 0.05), but significantly lower on days 16 and 
22. A similar pattern was observed in Control-1.25/MNBW-1.25 and 
Control-0/MNBW-0. These results suggest that MNBW facilitates hy­
drolysis, thereby accelerating VFAs production. As the AD process 
continued, MNBW accelerated the consumption of VFAs, thereby pre­
venting their accumulation.
The degradation of HPr is thermodynamically considered an unfav­
ourable reaction, and its accumulation is the primary cause of VFAs 
inhibition (Rocamora et al., 2023). To investigate the impact of MNBW 
on HPr degradation, the HPr concentration was measured across the 
different treatment groups, as illustrated in Fig. 1a and 1b. No statisti­
cally significant differences were observed between the RControl and 
RMNBW in the same HPr treatment group at the beginning of the AD 
process (p > 0.05). The HPr concentrations in Control-0/MNBW- 
0 initially increased before decreasing, with HPr concentrations 
remaining below 700 mg/L, indicating minimal HPr accumulation. 
Notably, MNBW-0 was significantly lower than Control-0 by 24.2 % on 
day 4 (p = 0.004 < 0.05), and 58.2 % on day 16 (p < 0.001). Further­
more, MNBW-1.25 exhibited significantly lower HPr concentrations 
than that in Control-1.25 on days 10 and 16. Specifically, MNBW-1.25 
was significantly lower than MNBW-1.25 by 21.0 % on day 10 (p =

demonstrated significantly lower HPr concentrations than that in 
Contol-2.5 on days 16 and 22 (p < 0.05). Among them, MNBW-1.25 was 
significantly lower than MNBW-1.25 by 10.7 % on day 16 (p = 0.006 <
0.05), and 12.6 % on day 22 (p = 0.002 < 0.05). Moreover, a 
pronounced enhancement of HPr degradation by MNBW-2.5 was 
observed on days 16 and 22, which occurred later than the effects seen 
with MNBW-1.25 and MNBW-0, indicating that as the concentration of 
HPr increased, the promoting effect of MNBW on HPr degradation 
diminished. Additionally, Control-5/MNBW-5 maintained HPr concen­
trations exceeding 4300 mg/L throughout the AD process, with no sta­
tistically significant differences between MNBW-5 and Control-5. This 
result showed that when the HPr concentration exceeded the threshold, 
MNBW failed to effectively accelerate HPr degradation. In summary, at 
low HPr concentrations (Initial HPr = 1.25 and 2.50 mg/L), MNBW 
significantly enhanced HPr degradation. However, as the HPr concen­
tration increased, this promoting effect gradually weakened. Once the 
HPr concentration surpassed the threshold, the supplementation of 
MNBW did not lead to effective degradation of HPr.
3.2. Biogas and methane production
The biogas production data obtained under varying degrees of HPr 
inhibition are shown in Fig. 2a. The maximum biogas production 
occurred in MNBW-2.5, reaching 909 ± 22 mL. This result showed an 
11.7 % increase relative to the Contol-2.5. The biogas yield of MNBW- 
1.25 was 824 ± 19 mL, reflecting a 13.3 % increase over that of the 
Control-1.25. In the absence of HPr inhibition, MNBW also enhanced 
biogas production, with MNBW-0 yielding 700 ± 15 mL, which is a 15.3 
% increase over that of the Control-0. The increase in biogas production 
attributable to MNBW across different HPr concentration treatment 
groups suggests that the promoting effect of MNBW diminished as the 
severity of HPr inhibition increased. Notably, biogas production in the 
Control-5/MNBW-5 groups was significantly reduced compared to the 
other groups, with no significant difference observed between MNBW-5 
and Control-5, indicating that MNBW does not significantly enhance 
biogas yield when the HPr concentration exceeded the threshold. The 
kinetic analysis results of biogas production process are shown in 
Table 2. The maximum biogas production potential and the maximum 
biogas production rate of MNBW-0, MNBW-1.25, and MNBW-2.5 were 
higher than those of the corresponding control group. Moreover, the lag 
phase of MNBW-0, MNBW-1.25, and MNBW-2.5 was shorter than that of 
the corresponding control group.
The trend of methane accumulation during the AD process mirrors 
that of biogas production (Fig. 2b). The cumulative methane yield of 
MNBW-0, MNBW-1.25, and MNBW-2.5 was 448 ± 8, 529 ± 10, and 601 
± 14 mL, respectively, indicating increases of 18.4 %, 18.3 %, and 13.5 
%, compared with Control-0, Control-1.25, and Contol-2.5, respectively. 
These results confirmed the promoting effect of MNBW on cumulative 
methane yield. The kinetic analysis results of methane production

MNBW-0, MNBW-1.25, and MNBW-2.5 was 22.38 ± 1.09, 21.15 ± 1.10, 
and 18.39 ± 1.22 mL/g-VS⋅d, respectively, indicating increases of 32.8 
%, 35.9 %, and 41.4 %, compared with Control-0, Control-1.25, and 
Contol-2.5, respectively. In addition, the maximum methane production 
potential of MNBW-0, MNBW-1.25, and MNBW-2.5 was also higher than 
that of the corresponding control group. Previous report has also indi­
cated that MNBW can enhance the methane yield (Fan et al., 2020). 
Compared to this previous report, the lower methane increment in this 
work was primarily because of the cost-saving decision to use Air- 
MNBW instead of H2-MNBW or other kinds of MNBW. The superior 
performance of H2-MNBW in promoting methane production may stem 
from its utilisation as a substrate by methanogens, thereby further 
increasing the methane yield.
Given identical substrate (raw SM) and inoculum loading, MNBW- 
2.5 achieved the highest biogas and methane yield, owing to the 
degradation and utilisation of HPr added to simulate inhibition at the 
beginning of the AD process. For Control-5/MNBW-5, the minimal 
degradation of HPr resulted in VFAs accumulation (VFAs concentrations 
exceeding 5000 mg/L), significantly affecting methane production. 
Furthermore, no statistically significant difference was observed be­
tween MNBW-5 and Control-5 in the methane yield (p > 0.05).
Subsequently, economic evaluation was applied in this work to 
better evaluate the economic potential of MNBW (see supplementary 
material). MNBW-0, MNBW-1.25 and MNBW-2.5 obtained 536.04, 
633.05 and 719.61 kWh of electric energy by processing 1 ton of SM, 
respectively, which were significantly higher than their corresponding 
control group (p < 0.05). These results indicate that NBW supplemen­
tation can significantly improve the economy of AD of SM under HPr 
inhibition. In addition, the electrical energy required for preparing 
MNBW to treat 1 ton of SM was calculated in this research. The MNBW

in one hour. The power consumption of MNBW generator in the process 
of treating 1 ton of SM was 10.33 kWh after calculation. Although the 
production of MNBW also consumes electrical energy, its consumption 
was much lower than its output. Therefore, under HPr inhibition, the 
approach of alleviating HPr inhibition and increasing methane pro­
duction by supplementing MNBW has economic value and is worthy of 
further study in the future.
In summary, the gas production performance of the reactors under 
different degrees of HPr inhibition indicated that as the level of HPr 
inhibition increased, the promoting effects of MNBW gradually dimin­
ished. In addition, the supplementation of MNBW significantly increased 
the methane production in AD of SM under HPr inhibition, which has 
economic value. MNBW failed to significantly enhance gas production 
when HPr concentrations exceeded the inhibition threshold.
3.3. Performance of the buffering capacity
The pH value is an important parameter in AD systems and serves as 
an indicator of system stability (Wu et al., 2022). The pH value of all 
bottles was tested throughout the AD process. The initial pH values 
differ among the reactor groups owing to the varying concentrations of 
HPr (Fig. 3a). Control-0/MNBW-0 and Control-1.25/MNBW-1.25 
exhibited an initial decline, followed by gradual increases, ultimately 
stabilising. The initial decline in pH was mainly due to the production of 
VFAs, whereas the subsequent increase in pH was due to the consump­
tion of VFAs. The pH of Contol-2.5/MNBW-2.5 increased gradually and 
stabilised, indicating that the AD process experienced initial HPr inhi­
bition, which was subsequently alleviated as VFAs were gradually 
consumed. Moreover, the pH of MNBW-2.5 on days 4, 10, and 16 were 
significantly higher than Contol-2.5. In contrast, MNBW-5 and Control-5 
were below 5.3 at the beginning of the AD process, and the pH remained 
below 6.2 throughout the AD process, suggesting HPr inhibition not 
being fully alleviated during the 34 days.
Alkalinity is a key indicator of the stability of AD systems and 
numerous studies have established its relationship with system stability 
(Zheng et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2023). Fig. 3b illustrates the changes in 
the total alkalinity (TA) content across all reactors. Control-5/MNBW-5 
exhibited the lowest TA content, approximately 1614 ± 63 mg CaCO3/L 
at the onset of the AD experiment, indicating a relatively poor buffering 
capacity. Conversely, Control-0/MNBW-0 had the highest TA content, 
followed by Control-1.25/MNBW-1.25 and Contol-2.5/MNBW-2.5. The 
TA levels increased in all groups, with Control-5/MNBW-5 consistently 
exhibiting significantly lower TA levels than the other groups, indicating 
poor stability. Notably, Control-0 were lower than MNBW-0 on days 4 
and 10, suggesting that MNBW contributed to increasing the TA levels. 
Similar patterns were observed for MNBW-1.25 and MNBW-2.5, which 
demonstrated higher TA levels than Control-1.25 and Contol-2.5 on days 
4, 10, 16 and on days 4, 10, respectively. Specifically, the TA content of 
MNBW-0, MNBW-1.25 and MNBW-2.5 on day 4 was 2740 ± 53, 2546 ±

41, and 2302 ± 44 mg CaCO3/L, respectively, indicating increases of 
4.8 %, 2.3 % and 4.7 %, compared with Control-0, Control-1.25, and 
Contol-2.5, respectively. These results indicate that, despite HPr inhi­
bition, MNBW aids in increasing TA levels, thus improving the buffering 
capacity.
The partial alkalinity (PA) parameter is also a significant indicator of 
AD system stability (Wu et al., 2021). The PA concentrations gradually 
increased and stabilised, mirroring the trend observed for TA (Fig. 3c). 
MNBW-0 showed a higher PA content than Control-0 on days 4 and 10. 
MNBW-0 was significantly higher than Control-0 by 10.6 % on day 4 (p 
= 0.001 < 0.05), and 6.3 % on day 10 (p = 0.046 < 0.05). Similarly, 
MNBW-1.25 and MNBW-2.5 displayed higher PA levels than the corre­
sponding control groups on days 10, 16, and 22. Specifically, MNBW- 
1.25 was higher than Control-1.25 by 2.8 % on day 10 (p = 0.464 >
0.05), 12.2 % on day 16 (p = 0.008 < 0.05), and 2.0 % on day 22 (p =
0.074 > 0.05). MNBW-2.5 was higher than Control-2.5 by 13.3 % on day 
10 (p = 0.018 < 0.05), 4.8 % on day 16 (p = 0.123 > 0.05), and 5.3 % on 
day 22 (p = 0.372 > 0.05). These findings suggest that MNBW facilitated 
alkalinity recovery under HPr inhibition conditions, thereby improving 
the buffering capacity in AD process.
To comprehensively evaluate the stability of the AD system, we 
introduced two additional assessment indicators: intermediate alkalinity 
(IA)/PA and VFA/TA, both of which are widely applied to assess the 
stability of AD systems (Feng et al., 2020). Fig. 3d shows the overall 
trend of IA/PA throughout the AD process, which gradually decreased 
before stabilisation. In the early phase of AD, the IA/PA ratios for 
Contol-2.5/MNBW-2.5 were both > 2.5, indicating a poor buffering 
capacity. The IA/PA ratio gradually fell below 1 by day 16, reflecting 
severe HPr inhibition. Compared to MNBW-2.5, Contol-2.5 was signifi­
cantly higher on days 10, 16, and 22 (p < 0.05). Specifically, Contol-2.5 
was significantly higher than MNBW-2.5 by 17.4 % on day 10 (p =
0.001 < 0.05), 9.1 % on day 16 (p = 0.042 < 0.05), and 7.8 % on day 22 
(p = 0.005 < 0.05), suggesting that MNBW aided in restoring the sta­
bility under severe HPr inhibition. Similar trends were observed for 
MNBW-1.25 and MNBW-0, which exhibited lower IA/PA ratios than 
Control-1.25 and Control-0 on days 10, 16, and on days 4, 10, respec­
tively. These results further indicate that MNBW helps reduce the IA/PA 
ratio under HPr inhibition.
The trends in VFA/TA values for all reactors are shown in Fig. 3e. The 
initial VFA/TA values for Contol-2.5/MNBW-2.5 and Control-5/MNBW- 
5 were both > 1.5, indicating poor stability during the early AD phase. 
The VFA/TA value for Control-1.25 was lower than MNBW-1.25 on day 
4, but higher on days 10 and 16, suggesting that MNBW facilitated VFAs 
production in the early stages and subsequently promoted HPr decom­
position and increased alkalinity. This result is consistent with the trends 
in HPr and VFAs concentrations observed in Fig. 1. The VFA/TA values 
for MNBW-2.5 were lower than Contol-2.5 on days 4, 16, and 22, further 
indicating that MNBW was beneficial to improve the buffering capacity 
in AD process.
In conclusion, these results indicate that MNBW is beneficial for 
restoring the buffering capacity in AD process. Enhanced system sta­
bility in the presence of HPr inhibition may be attributed to HPr 
degradation by MNBW, thereby preventing VFAs accumulation.
3.4. Soluble organics and TAN
This study focused on the dynamics of soluble carbohydrates and 
proteins to clarify the effect of MNBW on soluble organics under con­
ditions of HPr inhibition. Fig. 4a shows the behaviour of soluble car­
bohydrates throughout the AD process under varying degrees of HPr 
inhibition. The concentrations of soluble carbohydrates in Control-5/ 
MNBW-5 rapidly increased during the early hydrolysis phase of AD, 
but subsequently showed no significant consumption, indicating that 
severe HPr inhibition may have affected further degradation of soluble 
organics, such as carbohydrates. In Contol-2.5/MNBW-2.5, soluble 
carbohydrates accumulated during the early AD phase and were rapidly 
consumed later. This behaviour is due to the high concentration of HPr, 
which initially impeded the consumption of soluble carbohydrates. As 
HPr inhibition was gradually alleviated, these carbohydrates were uti­
lised. Notably, soluble carbohydrates in MNBW-2.5 were consistently 
lower than Contol-2.5 on days 28 and 34, suggesting that MNBW sup­
plementation accelerated the degradation of soluble organics, including 
carbohydrates. Specifically, MNBW-2.5 was lower than Control-2.5 by 
7.4 % on day 28 (p = 0.032 < 0.05), and 9.6 % on day 34 (p = 0.122 >
0.05). When the concentration of HPr was low, the consumption of 
soluble carbohydrates was not significantly inhibited, and the carbo­
hydrates rapidly decomposed during the early AD phase. These results 
further confirm that MNBW promotes the degradation and consumption 
of soluble carbohydrates under HPr inhibition. The trends in soluble 
protein concentrations across all reactors during AD are shown in 
Fig. 4b. In Control-5/MNBW-5, soluble proteins were not effectively 
consumed during AD. Conversely, the other groups showed an initial 
increase, followed by a decrease in soluble protein levels, which 
mirrored the changes observed in soluble carbohydrates.
To ascertain whether ammonia inhibition occurred, TAN concen­
trations were measured across all reactors. The TAN concentrations in 
all reactors increased gradually in the initial phase before stabilising, 
with no reactor exceeding 1400 mg/L (Fig. 4c). Preliminary results 
indicated that ammonia inhibition did not occur during the AD process 
and that the inhibiting factors in this work were attributed to HPr in­
hibition. Furthermore, the concentration of free ammonia nitrogen in all 
reactors remained below 50 mg/L throughout the AD process (Fig. 4d), 
further confirming the absence of significant ammonia inhibition.

3.5. Enzyme activity
Hydrolytic enzymes are particularly important in AD system (Pang 
et al., 2020). Furthermore, during methanogenesis, the activity of 
certain key enzymes substantially influences methanogen growth and 
methane yield (Li et al., 2024a). The activities of the four types of 
extracellular hydrolytic enzymes in MNBW-2.5 were significantly higher 
than those in the Contol-2.5 (The p values range from 0.002 to 0.023, 
less than 0.05), with increases ranging from 7.0 % to 13.8 % (Fig. 5a). 
Additionally, the activities of these extracellular hydrolytic enzymes in 
MNBW-1.25 and MNBW-0 were also significantly higher than those of 
Control-1.25 and Control-0, respectively, and the p values range from 
0.004 to 0.046, less than 0.05. These findings further validate the 
conclusion that MNBW enhances the extracellular hydrolytic enzyme 
activity in the presence of HPr inhibition. Moreover, the experimental 
results for coenzyme F420 illustrated that F420 activity in MNBW re­
actors was higher than control reactors (Fig. 5b). Specifically, the F420 
activity in MNBW-0 increased by 21.0 % compared to that in Control- 
0 (p = 0.001 < 0.05), which was greater than the increase observed 
for MNBW-1.25 (p = 0.019 < 0.05) and MNBW-2.5 (p = 0.001 < 0.05) 
relative to their respective control group. This suggests that HPr inhi­
bition are unfavourable for MNBW to enhance methanogen activity and 
methane production. These results reveal that despite HPr inhibition, 
MNBW could still promote hydrolysis and methanogenesis. Enhanced 
methanogens are better able to tolerate a certain concentration of VFAs 
and can convert VFAs, including HPr, into methane and carbon dioxide 
more quickly, thereby reducing the accumulation of HPr and easing the 
inhibition of VFAs (Li et al., 2021a).
3.6. Microbial community structure
To find out the reasons by which MNBW accelerates HPr degrada­
tion, alleviates HPr inhibition, and increases methane production, we 
compared the microbial community structure differences between the 
reactors with MNBW and control groups. Since the AD process of 
Control-5/MNBW-5 failed, the other six groups of samples were mainly 
concerned, namely Control-2.5/MNBW-2.5, Control-1.25/MNBW-1.25 
and Control-0/MNBW-0. In the control groups, the abundance of 
archaea and bacteria showed a downward trend with an increase in HPr, 
indicating the negative effect of HPr inhibition in RControl (see supple­
mentary material). Different from the control group, the bacterial 
abundance of MNBW-1.25 was higher than that of MNBW-0, indicating 
that MNBW can play a positive role in improving bacterial abundance 
when HPr inhibition is not serious. The bacterial abundance of MNBW- 
1.25, however, was lower than that of MNBW-2.5, suggesting that 
MNBW could not improve bacterial abundance when HPr inhibition was 
severe.
The dominant bacteria were Proteobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and Firmi­
cutes at the phylum level of bacteria (Fig. 6a). Reportedly, these mi­
croorganisms fermented with polysaccharide substances in the system 
and participated in biodegradation of macromolecular organics to pro­
vide a small molecular carbon source for methanogens (Strąpo´c et al., 
2011; Wu et al., 2024). Hydrogenophilaceae and Bacteroidetes_vadinHA17 
are participated in the denitrification and degradation of various com­
plex organics (Sun et al., 2015). Bacteroidetes_vadinHA17 used more 
polysaccharides and sterols in the system for acid production by 
fermentation and accelerates the reaction process (Baker et al., 2020).

The relative abundance (RA) of Bacteroidetes_vadinHA17 in MNBW-1.25 
was 8.8 %, which was higher than Control-1.25 by 76.2 %. Similarly, the 
RA of MNBW-2.5 (6.7 %) was higher than Control-2.5 by 97.0 %. These 
results suggest that MNBW promotes the consumption of proteoglycans 
and accelerates methane production. As for Hydrogenophilaceae, the RA 
of MNBW-0, MNBW-1.25 and MNBW-2.5 were 4.6 %, 1.2 % and 14.9 %, 
respectively, higher than those of the corresponding controls. Previous 
studies have shown that Sulfurovaceae and methanogens complement 
nutrient metabolism (Nie et al., 2021). Sulfurovaceae gradually 
decreased with increasing HPr in RMNBW and RControl (Fig. 6b), indicating 
that high HPr concentrations were not conducive to the nutritional 
metabolic pathways of methanogens, thereby inhibiting methane pro­
duction. In addition, Sulfurovaceae in MNBW-1.25 and MNBW-0 were 
higher than Control-1.25 and Control-0, respectively. Specifically, 
MNBW-0 (17.5 %) was higher than Control-0 by 36.7 %. Similarly, 
MNBW-1.25 was higher than Control-1.25 by 10.8 %. These results in­
dicates that MNBW supplementation is of positive significance for 
optimising the nutritional metabolic pathways of methanogens and 
increasing methane production when HPr inhibition is not severe.
In conclusion, Hydrogenophilaceae and Bacteroidetes_vadinHA17 were 
the dominant bacteria and contributed greatly to accelerating the con­
sumption of proteoglycans and promoting acidogenic methanogenesis. 
A higher concentration of HPr inhibited methane production, whereas 
MNBW relieved HPr inhibition, promoted proteoglycan consumption, 
and accelerated methane production.
The main archaeal phyla, including Halobacterota, Euryarchaeota, 
and Crenarchaeota were all methanogenic archaea (Yutin et al., 2008). 
Halobacterota had the largest proportion (18.3 %–44.5 %). Cren­
archaeota was the second most dominant species (6.4 %–22.1 %), 
whereas the proportion of Euryarchaeota was approximately 8.5 %–15.4 
% (Fig. 6c). As shown in Fig. 6d, the dominant species were Meth­
anosaetaceae, Methanobacteriaceae, unclassified_Bathyarchaeia, and 
Methanosaricinaceae. Methanosaetaceae was the most common species 
that produce methane from acetate (Smith and Ingram-Smith, 2007). It 
decreased gradually with an increase in HPr in RControl, indicating that 
high-concentration HPr inhibited Methanosaetaceae and caused sys­
tematic acidification, affecting the methane production process. The RA 
of Methanosaetaceae in MNBW-2.5 was 18.0 %, which was higher than 
that in Control-2.5 (2.3 %), suggesting that supplementing MNBW 
enhanced acetate consumption, thus alleviating inhibition and 
increasing methane production.
In conclusion, Halobacterota, Euryarchaeota, and Crenarchaeota are 
the three dominant methanogens. A high HPr concentration caused 
systematic acidification and affected the methanogenic process. Sup­
plementation with MNBW alleviates HPr inhibition to a certain extent. 
However, excessive HPr inhibited the abundance of acetic acid- 
methanogenic microorganisms.
3.7. Possible underlying mechanisms related to MNBW alleviating HPr 
inhibition
To clarify the underlying mechanisms by which MNBW alleviates 
HPr inhibition, the composition and characteristics of Air-MNBW and its 
role in accelerating HPr degradation and ultimately increasing methane 
production were analyzed in this work. As we all know, Air-MNBW is 
composed of water and air-MNBs, which mainly contain O2 and N2. 
Previous studies have shown that both O2-MNBW and N2-MNBW can 
promote AD process and increase methane production (Wang et al., 
2020, Yang et al., 2019). Although the introduction of O2 may contradict 
the anaerobic environment of AD, a number of reports have shown that 
O2-MNBW is conducive to the degradation of refractory organics and 
increase the activity of facultative bacteria, thus promoting the AD 
process and increasing methane production (Wang et al., 2021; Wang 
et al., 2023). In addition, studies have shown that the micro-oxygen 
environment is conducive to the AD process (Nguyen and Khanal, 
2018; Nguyen et al., 2019). Therefore, the introduction of O2 in Air- 
MNBs in this study may play a positive role in the AD process. As for 
MNBs, it has the characteristics of large specific surface area, strong 
stability and rich in free radicals. Its rupture releases physical energy 
(such as shear force) and produces a large number of reactive oxygen 
species, which is conducive to the degradation of refractory organics 
(Jia et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2019).
The composition of Air-MNBW determines that it has characteristics 
that DW does not have. It has higher spin–spin relaxation times, zeta 
potential and electron transport system (ETS) activity, etc, which makes 
MNBW have high mobility, strong solubility and high mass transfer ef­
ficiency (Chuenchart et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2019). The introduction of 
MNBs, O2 and water molecules with high mobility during AD could 
affect HPr inhibition. Firstly, in the hydrolysis stage of AD process, Air- 
MNBW improved the activity of hydrolase and promoted the degrada­
tion of soluble carbohydrates/proteins (Fig. 4 and Fig. 5). Subsequently, 
in the acidogenesis stage, the supplementation of Air-MNBW accelerated 
VFAs production (Fig. 1). After that, in the acetogenesis stage, Air- 
MNBW promoted the degradation of HPr to acetate (Fig. 1). Finally, in 
the methanogenesis stage, the supplementation of Air-MNBW increased 
the activity of key enzymes (such as F420) and methanogens (Fig. 5). 
Moreover, a previous study has shown that MNBW supplementation 
enhances the activity of hydrogenotrophic methanogens (HM) and 
acetoclastic methanogens (AM) (Wang et al., 2020). The increased ac­
tivity of HM and AM could tolerate the toxicity caused by a certain 
concentration of VFAs, accelerate the degradation of VFAs (including 
HPr), and alleviate the inhibition of HPr (Li et al., 2021a). In addition, 
previous studies have shown that the supplementation of MNBW can 
improve ETS activity and mass transfer efficiency (Chuenchart et al., 
2021; Temesgen et al., 2017). This result suggests that Air-MNBW may 
strengthen the DIET between methanogens and syntrophic bacteria, and 
is conducive to the mitigation of HPr inhibition. Further studies are 
needed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms by which MNBW alle­
viates HPr inhibition.
4. Conclusion
The role of MNBW in accelerating HPr degradation, enhancing 
methane production, and optimizing methanogenic pathways was sys­
tematically studied in this work. Results suggested that MNBW accel­
erated HPr degradation and improved system stability. In addition, 
cumulative methane production increased by 13.5 % to 18.4 % when 
MNBW was introduced compared with control group. Moreover, sup­
plementing MNBW boosted the activity of related enzymes. MNBW also 
optimised the microbial community structure and enhanced metha­
nogen tolerance to HPr inhibition. MNBW, being a pollution-free, 
chemical-free, and low-cost technology, does not require complex 
equipment or high energy consumption. As an environmentally friendly 
approach, MNBW offers a novel solution for addressing HPr-related in­
hibition, laying the foundation for broader industrial applications in 
waste treatment and bioenergy production, with significant potential for 
further development.
